full_judgment:
12. I had carefully gone through both the judgments of the courts below. It appears from the judgment by the trial Court that learned judge duly discussed and considered the evidences of both the sides and on a proper discussion and consideration of the evidences, he came to the positive finding that the pre-emptor failed to prove his alleged date of knowledge and the case is hopelessly barred by limitation. On reading the impugned judgment, it appears that the lower appellate Court disposed of the appeal in a very sweeping way. The appellate Court did not discuss the evidences adduced from the side of the pre-emptor but took much pain in discussing the evidences of the pre-emptor, of course, not in true perspective. The appellate Court shifted the burden of proof of the first date of knowledge upon the pre-emptee when he found that primary burden was upon the pre-emptee to prove that the pre-emptor was aware of the transfer of the case land prior to the date of knowledge alleged by him and also that case is barred by limitation. 

 13. In a proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the pre-emptor comes to the court to enforce a right of pre-emption. A period of limitation is prescribed by the statute for the said purpose. The burden lies upon the pre-emptor to prove the date of his alleged knowledge and that is also within the period of limitation. The pre-emptor is to succeed on the strength and proof of his own case. So, in order to get rid of the bar of limitation in cases where the same had been filed from a alleged date of knowledge, the pre-emptor is to prove the alleged date of knowledge by uncontroverted evidences. It is true that if pre-emptor proves his first date of knowledge, his initial onus is discharged and the onus is shifted upon the preemptee to know that the pre-emptor had earlier knowledge of the date as alleged by him as his first date of knowledge. In this instant case before me, the pre-emptor in the pre-emption case did not mention of any particular date of knowledge and there was also no averment from whom and from which source he became aware of the transfer in question. PW 2, Ayezuddin, who was made an informant in the evidence of pre-emptor also could not state the exact date when the alleged informant, for the first time, informed the kabala matter to the pre-emptor. This witness only stated that in the month of Falgun 1381 BS he informed the pre-emptor of the disputed kabala matter. There was no averment in the pre-emption case that OPW 2 Ayezuddin informed pre-emptor of the kabala matter and this evidence was beyond pleading. The pre-emptor cannot be allowed to give evidence to that effect when the said had not been pleaded in the pre-emption case. The provisions contained in Order 6 rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure is a standing bar. 

 16. Let me now consider the decisions referred to by Mr. MA Wahhab Mia, learned Advocate for the pre-emptor. In the case of Habibur Rahman Khalifa vs. Satish Chandra Gosh 29 DLR 178 the question of knowledge came up for consideration before the High Court Division. In that case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the alleged date of knowledge was on 1-4-1963 from one Alauddin and Abdus Sobhan. The learned Munsif on consideration of the materias on record rejected the pre-emption case holding that the application was barred by limitation. On appeal, the appellate Court affirmed the decision of the learned Munsif. Pre-emptor then moved this Court against the said decision and obtained the Rule. It was contended before the High Court Division that since the opposite party (pre-emptee) contended that the petitioner (pre-emptor) had prior knowledge it was for the opposite party (pre-emptee) to prove positively that the (pre-emptor) had such knowledge in order to knock out the claim of the petitioner (pre-emptor) on the ground of limitation. This contention was rejected by the High Court Division. Ranadhir Sen, J (as his Lordship then was) delivering the judgment observed that the burden lay on the pre-emptor to prove his alleged date of knowledge and the pre-emptor was to succeed on the strength of his own case. In that case what constitutes ''knowledge'' also came up for consideration. Ranadhir Sen, J took into consideration of a good number of authorities and observed that knowledge must be definite knowledge. A precise or exact perception of the necessary particulars of a fact is the determinant of knowledge which is essentially a question of fact. This case does not lend support to the contention of the learned Advocate Mr MA Wahhab Mia, rather the same negatived his contention.
